Phase 3 numbers preserved in 03-baseline.json as historical record; Phase 4 numbers represent current machine state used by the gate.
_meta.aggregation: median of 3 single-fork JMH runs (-f 1 -wi 3 -i 3 -w 1s -r 1s) — same Phase 3 methodology
_meta.tolerance_rationale: Phase 3 raised default from 15% to 50% due to hybrid P/E noise floor on i7-1255U; Phase 4 inherits the 50% standard. New streaming benchmarks also use 50% tolerance — they exercise chunked CSV reader + per-chunk aggregator merge, both with chunk-allocation overhead and iterator traversal costs within the same hybrid P/E envelope.
_meta.future_work: Phase 5 may pin to P-cores via /affinity or set up isolated benchmark profile. Until then, treat ±50% as the noise floor on this hardware.
_meta.phase4_re_measurement_note: Phase 4 re-measured all 10 perf benchmarks on the same machine using identical JMH config. Median numbers reflect current JVM state; Phase 3 numbers (in 03-baseline.json) showed the machine was running ~50% slower overall — likely thermal throttling / P-core scheduling differences across sessions. Both baseline files are valid; 04-baseline.json supersedes 03-baseline.json for the gate.

NEW — chunked read_csv over california_housing.csv (~20k rows, 2-3 chunks at 10k rows). Comparable to in-memory read_csv_california (58.064ms in same sweep): the BufferedReader per-chunk allocation + Series construction overhead is roughly equal to the in-memory single-shot parse cost at this dataset size. Expected to scale advantage only appears on larger files (>100k rows) where in-memory blows up but streaming stays constant memory.

NEW — streaming groupby via RunningGroupAggregator.sum over titanic.csv (~891 rows, single chunk). The 26ms cost is dominated by CsvChunkReader per-chunk parser overhead + Series materialization in the single-chunk case (the aggregator loop itself is O(n) and negligible). For multi-chunk merges the cost grows linearly with chunk count; for single-chunk the constant is high but not pathological.
